extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funds (school administrators, institutional legal counsel), education policymakers, and the public/commenters on Title IX rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and legal interpretation of the scope and authority of 34 C.F.R. §106.10, addressing which bases of discrimination Title IX covers and the Department's rationale for the final regulatory text. Geared toward implementers, litigators, and stakeholders assessing compliance and legal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.10 clarifies scope of Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department agrees that §106.10 will promote nondiscriminatory educational environments by clarifying the scope of Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination and expects that §106.10 will facilitate a consistent understanding of Title IX across the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision is intended to help ensure recipients, students, and the public understand how the Department interprets Title IX; it is framed to provide notice of the broad scope of prohibited sex discrimination without specifying outcomes for all factual scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of specific bases in §106.10
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations clarify that Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination includes discrimination on the basis of sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy or related conditions, sexual orientation, and gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each basis is described and justified in the NPRM and preamble; the Department relies on case law (e.g., Bostock, Price Waterhouse, Grimm, Grabowski) to support inclusion and explains that each basis necessarily involves consideration of a person's sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to define 'sex' in §106.10
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department determined it is not necessary to define each of the bases of discrimination listed in §106.10 or other related preamble terms; the Department has defined key terms as necessary in §106.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terms used are described in the preamble for convenience and explanation but need not be defined in §106.10 for application of the final regulations; recipients may, if they choose, further clarify terms in local policies or training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bases listed in §106.10 are illustrative, not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble explains that the listed bases are intended to provide recipients notice of the broad scope of prohibited sex discrimination and that the bases listed are not exhaustive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is deliberate to reflect Title IX's broad prohibition on discrimination 'on the basis of sex'; recipients seeking additional clarity may adopt policies or provide training that include examples of prohibited conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'bases' of discrimination and 'forms' of discriminatory conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.10 describes bases of discrimination that involve consideration of sex; sex-based harassment and sexual violence are examples of discriminatory conduct (forms), not bases themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is reflected in the definition of 'sex-based harassment' in §106.2 which states that harassment on the basis of sex is a 'form' of sex discrimination and includes harassment on the 'bases' listed in §106.10; therefore the regulatory text keeps bases and forms separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage includes discrimination based on perceived status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department agrees that §106.10 extends to discrimination based on a perceived status, whether the perception is accurate or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites Title VII and federal cases (e.g., Abercrombie & Fitch Stores; Roberts v. Glenn Indus.; Grabowski) to show courts recognize perceived-characteristic discrimination as unlawful; inclusion of sex stereotypes underscores that Title IX covers discrimination based on perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory interpretations are supported by federal case law and statute
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department relies on the text of Title IX and federal case law (e.g., Bostock, Price Waterhouse, Oncale, Davis, Gebser) to interpret 'on the basis of sex' broadly and to justify coverage of the bases included in §106.10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains the alignment with Supreme Court and circuit precedent, and that Title IX's plain terms provide notice to recipients; cited decisions inform that statutory prohibitions can cover reasonably comparable evils and support the Department's regulatory approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with Executive Order 12866 and need for regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued §106.10 did not meet Executive Order 12866 criteria; the Department disagrees and finds persistence of discrimination on listed bases presents a compelling public need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department asserts §106.10 will help ensure understanding of Title IX and that commenters provided evidence of prevalence and harmful effects of such discrimination, which OCR enforcement experience reinforces.

rubrics_metrics.name: PPRA does not prohibit §106.10's coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department disagrees that prohibitions on discrimination based on gender identity, sexual orientation, sex stereotypes, and sex characteristics violate the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PPRA requires parental consent for certain surveys and privacy protections (20 U.S.C. 1232h); the Department notes §106.10 does not require recipients to administer surveys or force disclosure of sex behavior/attitudes, and §106.6(g) reinforces legal rights of parents/guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marital status is not added as a separate prohibited 'basis' under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to add marital status to §106.10 because Title IX does not prohibit discrimination based on marital status per se since it does not necessarily require consideration of a person's sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, Title IX prohibits applying rules concerning marital status that treat individuals differently on the basis of sex (e.g., treating married women differently than married men); cross-references: 34 CFR 106.21(c), 106.37(a)(3), 106.40(a), 106.57(a), 106.60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations provide adequate notice without defining every scenario
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department maintains that the final regulations provide adequate notice of the scope of a recipient's legal obligations without purporting to specify outcomes for all scenarios, many of which will turn on particular facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other sections of the regulations address specific requirements and prohibitions; recipients retain ability to further clarify via policies/training; nothing requires restriction of constitutional rights under §106.6(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Department's statutory authority to promulgate Title IX regulations (20 U.S.C. 1682)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department states its authority to issue regulations governing equal opportunity under Title IX is well established (20 U.S.C. 1682 and other statutes) and that rulemaking here is within its delegated authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites statutory grants and Supreme Court precedent recognizing administrative enforcement mechanisms and the Department's power to effectuate Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final regulations are not applied retroactively
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will not—and does not have the authority to—enforce these final regulations retroactively; they apply only to sex discrimination that allegedly occurred on or after August 1, 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses commenters' concerns about retroactive imposition of new conditions on recipients who previously accepted Federal funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal regulations may preempt conflicting State laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department notes that the obligation to comply with Title IX and these final regulations is not obviated by State or local laws that conflict with Title IX; State laws can be preempted when impossible to comply with both or they obstruct federal objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites preemption principles and cases (e.g., Freightliner Corp., Hillsborough Cnty.); however, the Department refrains from opining about specific State laws without evaluating facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may adopt policies/training to clarify Title IX coverage locally
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent recipients want to further clarify the scope of discrimination under Title IX and these regulations, nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from adopting policies that include examples of prohibited conduct or providing training to its community on the scope of Title IX's coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an implementation option to help local communities understand obligations and to reduce concerns about vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations do not require restriction of First Amendment rights
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.6(d) makes clear that nothing in the Title IX regulations requires a recipient to restrict rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution, such as by restricting constitutionally protected speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that no provision authorizes suppression of constitutional rights and that the regulations provide adequate notice of obligations without infringing First Amendment protections.
